strengths: The paper addresses a critical and often overlooked methodological gap in audio chaptering: the mismatch between continuous-time chapter boundaries and discrete, transcript-dependent text-segmentation evaluation metrics.

The formalization of time-space evaluation protocols (T1 and T2) provides a standardized, transcript-invariant evaluation framework that enables fair comparisons across text-based, audio-only, and multimodal models.

The empirical analysis is remarkably thorough and highly structured, systematically comparing three modeling paradigms (text-based baseline, hand-crafted acoustic augmentation, audio-only models, and multimodal LLMs) across different video durations and speaker regimes.

The novel audio-only model, AudioSeg, demonstrates outstanding performance, showing that learned speech representations (especially from Whisper Large) can substantially outperform text-based pipelines without requiring transcription.
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation is limited to a single dataset (YTSeg). Although the authors correctly note in the limitations that YTSeg is the only publicly available large-scale dataset for this task, a small-scale out-of-domain evaluation on a manual subset from other speech corpora would have significantly strengthened the generalizability claims.

The choice of the discretization interval (the 6-second chunk size for ∆t) is motivated by the average sentence length of YTSeg, but the paper lacks a sensitivity analysis showing how varying ∆t affects the metrics and rankings.

The distinction between acoustic-only signals and speech-representing signals could be more clearly articulated; the top-performing encoder (Whisper Large) relies heavily on linguistic features implicitly encoded during ASR pretraining, which blurs the line between purely acoustic cues and text-centric semantic cues.

strengths: The paper identifies and addresses a key methodological limitation in current audio chaptering research—the heavy dependency on transcript-space discretization (such as sentence boundaries)—by formalizing and proposing transcript-invariant evaluation protocols (T1 and T2).

Introduces a novel and highly effective audio-only model (AudioSeg) that operates directly on learned speech representations, demonstrating that acoustic cues alone can substantially outperform traditional text-only pipelines on the YTSeg dataset.

Provides a thorough, multi-dimensional empirical analysis of the impact of various factors (including pause duration, speaker changes, video duration, and transcript quality), offering valuable insights into what drives segmentation performance.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, clearly structured, and supports reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, prompt designs, and a commitment to release the code and model checkpoints.
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation is restricted to a single dataset (YTSeg). Although the authors note this is the only large-scale public English dataset available for the task, testing the proposed approaches on an out-of-domain subset or another smaller corpus would further validate the generalizability of the findings.

While the continuous-time evaluation protocol (T2) is formalized in Section 2, the main experimental comparisons in the paper rely on the discretized T1 protocol. Providing results under the continuous T2 protocol would make the empirical validation of the proposed metrics more robust.

The main proposed models (MiniSeg + features and AudioSeg) focus entirely on boundary detection, whereas real-world chaptering entails generating chapter titles. While this is touched upon in the MLLM experiments, a brief discussion on how the boundary models can be integrated with title-generation modules in a complete pipeline would enhance the practical value of the work.

strengths: Well-motivated and structured critique of the current text-centric evaluation protocols for audio chaptering, addressing a major methodological flaw where standard metrics are biased by ASR segmentation differences.

Highly comprehensive and rigorous experimentation covering four major paradigms: text-based, text + hand-crafted acoustic features, audio-only (with six different self-supervised/weakly-supervised encoders), and multimodal LLMs (under zero-shot, ICL, cascaded, and LoRA settings).

Valuable empirical insights, such as isolating the specific impact of pauses, analyzing the performance under different speaker regimes (single vs. multi-speaker), and demonstrating the inherent discretization loss in text-space projection protocols via oracle testing.
Clear, precise writing with extensive details, hyperparameters, and prompts provided in the appendix, ensuring high reproducibility.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to a single dataset (YTSeg) in English. Testing on at least one additional corpus (even of a smaller scale) would greatly strengthen the generalizability of the findings.

The definition and interpretation of 'audio-only' models (AudioSeg) is somewhat blurred by the choice of encoder. The best results are achieved using Whisper Large, which is trained with text supervision and implicitly encodes strong linguistic structures. When using purely self-supervised representations (like HuBERT), the performance falls below the text-only baseline, suggesting that semantic information remains the primary driver of performance.

The continuous-time evaluation protocol (T2) is proposed as a key contribution in Section 2, but it is largely absent from the main empirical comparisons (Tables 4-7 focus entirely on the discrete-time T1 protocol).

The architectural novelty of the proposed AudioSeg model is relatively limited, as it represents a straightforward combination of existing frozen audio encoders, local transformers, and RoFormer sequence labelers. The contribution is heavily methodological and empirical rather than architectural.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant limitation in existing audio chaptering research by formalizing transcript-invariant, time-space evaluation protocols (T1 and T2). This provides a solid methodological foundation for future research.

A comprehensive set of experiments systematically compares multiple modeling paradigms: text-based, text augmented with acoustic features, a novel audio-only architecture (AudioSeg), and state-of-the-art multimodal LLMs.

The empirical findings are highly insightful, demonstrating that audio-only models can outperform text-based ones, that pause duration is the most critical hand-crafted acoustic cue, and that MLLMs struggle with precise temporal grounding.
The paper is very well-written, clearly structured, and provides extensive analyses, including ablation studies, domain generalization on AMI, and failure analysis of MLLMs.
weaknesses: The evaluation is largely centered on a single main dataset (YTSeg), with the out-of-domain evaluation on the AMI meeting corpus being relatively small-scale.

While the paper contrasts audio-only (AudioSeg) and text-only models, the combination of deep learned audio representations with textual sentence embeddings in a dedicated hybrid/fusion architecture (beyond MLLMs or hand-crafted features) is not fully explored.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical methodological gap in audio chaptering research by formalizing and contrasting text-space vs. time-space evaluation protocols. The introduction of transcript-invariant protocols (T1 and T2) enables a fair, unified comparison across text-based, audio-only, and multimodal models.

It conducts a highly comprehensive and systematic benchmarking of four distinct paradigms: text-only, text augmented with acoustic features, a novel audio-only model (AudioSeg), and state-of-the-art MLLMs (Qwen-Omni series) across various inference strategies.

The proposed audio-only model (AudioSeg) utilizing Whisper Large representations achieves outstanding performance (45.52 F1), significantly outperforming text-based approaches and illustrating that learned audio representations encode vital structural cues (e.g., pauses, non-speech transitions) that transcripts omit.

The paper offers exceptionally detailed and insightful empirical analyses, diagnosing model performance based on audio duration, speaker regimes, transcript qualities, and cross-domain transferability on the AMI meeting corpus.
weaknesses: While AudioSeg is structurally an audio-only model, its top-performing variant relies on a Whisper Large encoder. Since Whisper is trained with ASR supervision, it implicitly encodes linguistic structures. The paper would benefit from a more explicit disentanglement of how much of this success is driven by implicit text representations vs. acoustic cues.

The experimental evaluation is largely centered on the English-only YTSeg dataset. Although out-of-domain transfer is validated on the AMI corpus, exploration of multilingual applicability remains limited.

Due to computational constraints, full-parameter fine-tuning of the strongest and largest MLLMs (e.g., Qwen3-Omni) was not explored, which limits the optimization potential of the multimodal baseline.

strengths: Provides a much-needed methodological formalization of evaluation protocols for audio chaptering, distinguishing text-space and time-space protocols and highlighting the discretization errors inherent in transcript-based evaluation.

Presents a comprehensive and systematic empirical comparison across four distinct paradigms: text-only, audio-augmented text, a novel audio-only architecture (AudioSeg), and state-of-the-art multimodal large language models (MLLMs).

Reveals highly valuable and actionable insights for the community, such as the fact that ASR quality (WER) does not directly correlate with text-based chaptering performance, and that pause features drive the vast majority of acoustic gains in text-audio hybrid models.

Proposes 'AudioSeg', an audio-only model which significantly outperforms text-based baselines, showcasing the power of self-supervised speech representations (such as Whisper Large features) to capture structural cues directly from raw audio.
Strong commitment to open science and reproducibility by releasing an evaluation toolkit, augmented dataset annotations (duration and speaker regimes), and model code.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty of AudioSeg is relatively limited, as it primarily represents a combination of established components (such as frozen speech encoders, local segment transformers, and RoFormer document encoders) rather than a fundamentally new modeling technique.
The evaluation of Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) is constrained to videos under 30 minutes due to context length limits, which is a significant drawback for a task intended specifically for long-form audio.

While the paper advocates strongly for continuous-time evaluation (T2) to avoid discretization artifacts, the primary evaluation across most tables and figures still relies on the discrete-time (T1) 6-second chunk setup, slightly undermining the continuous-time framework's adoption as the primary standard.
